content: Fever is a common symptom in malaria, and both pharmacological interventions (antipyretic drugs) and physical methods (such as sponging) are frequently employed to provide symptomatic relief. However, some researchers have hypothesized that reducing fever might potentially prolong the duration of malaria illness. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether interventions aimed at reducing fever in malaria patients have any impact on the progression or resolution of the disease. To address this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Trial Register (as of June 2012), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (Issue 6, 2012), MEDLINE (from 1966 to June 2012), EMBASE (from 1980 to June 2012), and LILACS (June 2012). Additionally, researchers and organizations involved in malaria research were contacted to identify unpublished or ongoing trials. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated fever-reducing interventions in adults or children with confirmed malaria. Two authors independently applied these criteria to select studies for inclusion. Data from eligible trials were extracted using a standardized form, and mean differences with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for continuous outcomes. The GRADE approach was employed to assess and summarize the quality of the evidence. A total of ten randomized controlled trials, involving 990 participants (both adults and children), met the inclusion criteria. These trials were small in scale, had methodological limitations, and were conducted in diverse patient populations. Some studies reported that antipyretic drugs influenced the time required for fever to resolve, while others found no such effect. Regarding parasite clearance, no consistent or significant impact of fever-reducing interventions was observed (based on six trials with 423 participants, with the evidence rated as very low quality). Furthermore, there was no observed difference in the frequency or severity of adverse events between participants receiving antipyretic drugs and those in the control groups. In conclusion, the available evidence does not provide clarity on whether antipyretic interventions affect the time required for parasite clearance in malaria. Determining whether further trials are warranted to explore this question would depend on the perceived importance of resolving this issue through interventional research.
